(Surat al-Humazah)
Nine verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter.﴾ In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter.﴾ In this there are several issues:

The first issue: *al-Wayl* (woe) is a word of censure and condemnation. It is the expression of anyone in distress who turns away and calls out "woe." Its origin is *wai li-fulan* (woe to so-and-so), and then it became so common in their speech that it was joined with the *lam*. It is also narrated that it is a mountain in Hell. If it is asked: why does he say here *wayl* (woe) and in another place, ﴿And woe to you﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 18]? We say: because there they said, ﴿O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 14], so He said, ﴿And woe to you﴾. Here He used it indefinite, because none knows its true reality except God. It has also been said that *wayl* is a word of disgust, *way*s is a word of belittling, and *way*h is a word of pity. Thus He alerts, by this, to the ugliness of this act. Scholars differ regarding the threat in this surah: does it include everyone who adopts this manner in evil deeds, or is it specific to particular people? The verifying scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*) said that it is general for everyone who commits this act, whoever he may be, because the specific cause does not detract from the generality of the wording. Others said that it is specific to certain people. Then ʿAṭāʾ and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who used to find fault with people and backbite them, especially the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who used to backbite the Prophet (ﷺ) behind his back and attack him to his face. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "We have always heard that this surah was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Khalaf." Al-Farra' said: that the wording is general does not preclude that its intended reference is a specific person, just as if a person said to you, "I will never visit you," and you say, "Whoever does not visit me, I will not visit him," while you intend by this general sentence only that person. This is what is called in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence) the restriction of the general by contextual indication (*takhsis al-‘amm bi-qarinat al-‘urf*).

[Page 87]

The second issue: *al-hamz* is breaking. God says, ﴿a backbiter, a gossip-monger﴾ [al-Qalam: 11]. *Al-lamz* is defamation. The intended meaning is breaking people's honor, belittling them and attacking them. God says, ﴿And do not find fault with one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. The form of the verb indicates that this is a habit of his to which he has become accustomed. Similar to these are *al-lu‘anah* (one who curses habitually) and *al-duhakah* (one who laughs habitually). It is also read: ﴿Woe to every *humzah lumzah*﴾ with the *mim* sukun (*lumzah* read as *lumzh*? i.e., with the *mim* unvowelled), and this refers to the buffoon who brings forth absurdities and jokes, so that he is laughed at and insulted. The commentators have several statements:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-humazah* is the one who backbites, and *al-lumazah* is the one who finds fault.

The second: Abu Zayd said: *al-humazah* is with the hand, and *al-lumazah* is with the tongue.

The third: Abu al-ʿAliyah said: *al-humazah* is to a person's face, and *al-lumazah* is behind his back.

The fourth: *al-humazah* is openly, and *al-lumazah* is secretly, with the eyebrow and the eye.

The fifth: *al-humazah* and *al-lumazah* is one who gives people nicknames they dislike. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah used to do this. However, this does not befit the rank of leadership; it is rather the habit of vulgar people. It includes whoever imitates people in their words, actions and voices in order to make them laugh. Al-Hakam ibn al-ʿAs imitated the gait of the Prophet (ﷺ), so he banished him from Medina and cursed him.

The sixth: al-Hasan said: *al-humazah* is one who pricks his companion, breaking his eye (i.e., by his glance), and *al-lumazah* is one who mentions his brother with evil and defames him.

The seventh: on the authority of Abu al-Jawza', who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter﴾ — who are those whom God condemns with woe?" He said: "They are those who walk about spreading tale-bearing, who sow discord among loved ones, who attribute defects to people."

Know that all these meanings are close to each other and return to one root, which is defamation and the display of faults. Then this is of two kinds: it may be in earnest, as occurs with envy and rancor, or it may be in jest, as occurs with mockery and making people laugh. Each of the two kinds may concern a matter related to religion, which is what relates to form, or to walking, or to sitting. Its types are numerous and not restricted. Then the display of faults in these four categories may be directed at someone present, or at someone absent, and in either case it may be by speech, or by a gesture of the head, the eye, or other things. All of this falls under the prohibition and the deterrent. The only question is: for what is the word, according to the language, originally established? Whatever the word is established for is forbidden according to the wording, and whatever the word is not established for is included in the prohibition according to clear analogy (*al-qiyas al-jali*). Since the Messenger was the greatest of people in rank in religion, defaming him was great in the sight of God. Therefore, undoubtedly, He said: ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter.﴾

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who gathers wealth and counts it﴾. On this verse there are two issues.

**The first issue:** The word ﴿الَّذِي﴾ (alladhī, "who") is either a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for the preceding word, or it is in the *naṣb ʿalā dhamm* (accusative of censure). God described him with this attribute because it functions as the cause and reason for the *hamz* (slandering) and *lamz* (defaming), namely his self-admiration at the wealth he has gathered and his belief that his superiority lies in that wealth, so he belittles others.

**The second issue:** Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ibn ʿĀmir recited ﴿جَمَّعَ﴾ (jammaʿa, with shaddah), while the rest recited ﴿جَمَعَ﴾ (jamaʿa, without shaddah). The meaning of *jammaʿa* and *jamaʿa* is one and the same, and they are close in meaning. The difference is that *jammaʿa* with the shaddah indicates that he gathered it from here and there, and that he did not gather it in one day, nor in two days, nor in one month or two months. One says: "So-and-so gathers wealth (yujammiʿu al-amwāl)," meaning he gathers it from here and there. As for *jamaʿa* without the shaddah, it does not indicate this.

As for His saying ﴿مالًا﴾ (mālan, "wealth"), the indefiniteness (*tankīr*) in it may have two interpretations:

The first: The word *māl* is a name for everything in this world, as He said: ﴿The wealth and the children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. So the wealth of one person, compared with the wealth of the whole world, is insignificant. How, then, is it fitting for him to boast of that little?

The second: The intended meaning is glorification, that is, wealth that has reached the utmost limits of corruption and ruin. How, then, is it fitting for the sensible person to boast of it?

As for His saying ﴿وَعَدَّدَهُ﴾ (waʿaddadahu, "and counts it"), there are several interpretations:

The first: It is derived from *ʿuddah*, which means a store or reserve. One says: "I prepared the thing for such-and-such (aʿdadtu al-shayʾ li-kadhā)" and "I counted it (ʿaddadtuhu)" when you hold it back for that purpose and make it a provision and reserve against the calamities of time.

The second: *ʿaddadahu* means he counted it, that is, he enumerated it. The doubling (*tashdīd*) is for the large number of the things counted, as one says: "So-and-so enumerates the virtues of so-and-so (yuʿaddidu faḍāʾil fulān)." For this reason al-Suddī said: "And ʿaddadahu means he counted it. He says: 'This is mine, and this is mine,' his wealth occupies him by day, and when night comes he hides it."

The third: *ʿaddadahu* means he multiplied it. One says: "Among the sons of so-and-so there is ʿadad (a large number)," meaning abundance. The last two opinions go back to the meaning of *ʿadad* (number), and the third opinion goes back to the meaning of *ʿuddah* (reserve).

Some recited ﴿وَعَدَدَهُ﴾ (waʿadadahu, without shaddah), and in this there are two interpretations:

The first: The meaning is that he gathered the wealth and controlled its number and counted it.

The second: He gathered his wealth and the number of his people who support him, from your saying: "So-and-so has ʿadad and ʿudad (a large following)" when he has a large number of helpers. A man who is like this is more inclined to boast.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 104, verses 3–4:

Then He, exalted is He, described him with another kind of ignorance, saying: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal.﴾

Know that akhladahu (أخلده) and khalladahu (خلّده) carry one meaning. Then, regarding the interpretation, there are several views:

The first: It is possible that the meaning is that the length of his hope (amal) for wealth, until he became, due to his extreme heedlessness and the length of his hope, one who thinks that his wealth has left him eternal in this world, not dying. He said "akhladahu" and did not say "yukhalliduhu" because the intended meaning is: this person thinks that wealth has guaranteed him immortality and given him security from death, as if it were a decree that has already been concluded, and for this reason it is mentioned in the past tense. Al-Hasan said: "I have never seen a certainty without doubt more akin to a doubt without certainty than death."

The second: He does deeds that are firmly built, such as erecting buildings with baked brick and plaster, like the deed of one who thinks he will remain alive, or in order that he be remembered through them after death.

The third: He loved wealth with an intense love, so much so that he believed: if my wealth decreases, I will die. Therefore he preserves it from loss so that he may remain alive. This is not far from the belief of the miser.

The fourth: This is an allusion to righteous deeds, and that it is they which make their doer immortal in this world through a good remembrance, and in the Hereafter through lasting bliss.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nay﴾ (kalla), there are two views concerning it:

One of them: It is a restraint for him from his assumption, meaning: the matter is not as he supposes, that wealth makes him immortal; rather, knowledge and righteousness do. From this is the saying of Ali, peace be upon him: "The keepers of wealth have died while they are alive, and the scholars remain as long as time remains."

The second view: its meaning is "truly" (haqqan), and the lam in ﴿surely he will be thrown﴾ (la-yunbadhanna) is the answer to an implied oath, and so the sense of an oath is conveyed by "kalla."

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Surely he will be thrown into the Crusher.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Crusher is?﴾ He mentioned it with the word nabdh (throwing), which indicates humiliation, because the disbeliever used to believe that he was among the people of honour. It was recited as "la-yunbadhan," meaning he and his wealth, and "la-yunbadhunna" with a dhamma on the dhal, meaning he and his helpers. As for "al-Hutama," al-Mubarrad said: it is the fire that crushes everyone who falls into it. A man is called hutama, meaning one who eats greedily, consuming the provisions of the people. The root meaning of al-hatm in the language is breaking, and it is said: "the worst of shepherds is the hutama," and one says: "ra'in hutama" and "hutam" without a ta' marbuta, as if he breaks the livestock, meaning he breaks them when driving them because of his harshness. The exegetes said: al-Hutama is one of the names of the Fire, and it is the second rank of the ranks of the Fire. Muqatil said: it crushes the bones and devours the flesh until it reaches the hearts.

﴿And what will make you know what the Hutamah is?﴾ ﴿It is the fire of Allah, kindled,﴾ ﴿which rises over the hearts.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them,﴾ ﴿in extended columns.﴾ Know that the benefit of naming Hell (Jahannam) by this name here has several aspects:

The first: the correspondence in form. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, says: "If you are a hummazah lumazah (a backbiter and slanderer), then behind you is the Hutamah."

The second: the one who slanders (al-hammaz) lowers the status of others and casts them into the depths. So Allah says: "Behind you is the Hutamah." In hatm (crushing) there is breaking. The Hutamah breaks you and casts you into the depths of Hell. But the hamzah (slander) is nothing more than breaking with the eyebrow, whereas the Hutamah breaks with a breaking that leaves nothing and spares nothing.

The third: the slanderer and backbiter eats the flesh of people, and al-Hutamah is also a name for the Fire, insofar as it consumes skin and flesh. It may be said: He mentioned two attributes, hamz and lamz, then countered them with a single name and said: "Take one from me in exchange for the two from you, for it suffices and fulfills." It is as if a questioner asks: "How can one suffice in place of two?" So He says: "You say this only because you do not know this one. Therefore, ﴿And what will make you know what the Hutamah is?﴾"

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the fire of Allah﴾, the idafah (genitive construction) is for glorification, meaning: it is a fire unlike other fires. ﴿Kindled﴾ means that which never goes out, ever. Or: kindled by His command, or by His power. From this is the saying of Ali, peace be upon him: "How strange is one who disobeys Allah upon the face of the earth while the Fire is kindled beneath him!" And in a hadith: "It was kindled for a thousand years until it turned red, then a thousand years until it turned white, then a thousand years until it turned black, so it is now black and dark."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿which rises over the hearts﴾: know that it is said: "He rose (ṭalaʿa) over the mountain and ascended (iṭṭalaʿa) upon it" when he climbed it. Then there are two interpretations of the verse:

The first: the Fire enters their bodies until it reaches their chests and rises over their hearts. Nothing in the human body is more delicate than the heart (al-fu'ad), and none is more pained by the slightest harm touching it. How much more so when the fire of Hell rises over it and overpowers it. Yet the heart, despite the Fire's domination over it, does not burn, for if it burned it would die. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Neither dying therein nor living﴾ [al-A'la 87:13]. The meaning of ittilaʿ (rising over) is that the Fire descends from the flesh to the heart.

The second: the reason the hearts are singled out for this is that they are the seats of disbelief, of corrupt beliefs, and of corrupt intentions. Know also that it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "The Fire consumes its people until, when it rises over their hearts, it stops. Then Allah, exalted is He, restores their flesh and bones a second time."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾, al-Hasan said: "Mu'sadah" means "closed," from aṣadtu al-bāba and awṣadtuhu, which are two dialects. He did not say "muṭbaqah" (sealed/covered), because al-mu'sadah refers to closed doors, and sealing (al-ițbāq) does not convey the meaning of a door.

Know that the verse conveys intensification of punishment in several respects:

The first: His saying "ليُنْبَذَنَّ" (they will surely be thrown, [al-Humazah 104:4]) implies that it is a place with a very deep bottom, like a well.

The second: had He willed, He could have made that place without any door. But by having a door, it reminds them of the possibility of exit, which increases their grief.

The third: He said ﴿upon them, closed﴾ and did not say "closed upon them." Because His saying ﴿ʿalayhim muʾṣadah﴾ indicates that the primary intent is their being in this state, whereas "muʾṣadah ʿalayhim" does not convey this meaning as the primary intent.

The first: His saying "ليُنْبَذَنَّ" (they will surely be thrown, [al-Humazah 104:4]) implies that it is a place with a very deep bottom, like a well.

The second: had He willed, He could have made that place without any door. But by having a door, it reminds them of the possibility of exit, which increases their grief.

The third: He said ﴿upon them, closed﴾ and did not say "closed upon them." Because His saying ﴿ʿalayhim muʾṣadah﴾ indicates that the primary intent is their being in this state, whereas "muʾṣadah ʿalayhim" does not convey this meaning as the primary intent.

﴿And what will make you know what the Hutamah is?﴾ ﴿It is the fire of Allah, kindled,﴾ ﴿which rises over the hearts.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them,﴾ ﴿in extended columns.﴾ Know that the benefit of naming Hell (Jahannam) by this name here has several aspects:

The first: the correspondence in form. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, says: "If you are a hummazah lumazah (a backbiter and slanderer), then behind you is the Hutamah."

The second: the one who slanders (al-hammaz) lowers the status of others and casts them into the depths. So Allah says: "Behind you is the Hutamah." In hatm (crushing) there is breaking. The Hutamah breaks you and casts you into the depths of Hell. But the hamzah (slander) is nothing more than breaking with the eyebrow, whereas the Hutamah breaks with a breaking that leaves nothing and spares nothing.

The third: the slanderer and backbiter eats the flesh of people, and al-Hutamah is also a name for the Fire, insofar as it consumes skin and flesh. It may be said: He mentioned two attributes, hamz and lamz, then countered them with a single name and said: "Take one from me in exchange for the two from you, for it suffices and fulfills." It is as if a questioner asks: "How can one suffice in place of two?" So He says: "You say this only because you do not know this one. Therefore, ﴿And what will make you know what the Hutamah is?﴾"

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the fire of Allah﴾, the idafah (genitive construction) is for glorification, meaning: it is a fire unlike other fires. ﴿Kindled﴾ means that which never goes out, ever. Or: kindled by His command, or by His power. From this is the saying of Ali, peace be upon him: "How strange is one who disobeys Allah upon the face of the earth while the Fire is kindled beneath him!" And in a hadith: "It was kindled for a thousand years until it turned red, then a thousand years until it turned white, then a thousand years until it turned black, so it is now black and dark."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿which rises over the hearts﴾: know that it is said: "He rose (ṭalaʿa) over the mountain and ascended (iṭṭalaʿa) upon it" when he climbed it. Then there are two interpretations of the verse:

The first: the Fire enters their bodies until it reaches their chests and rises over their hearts. Nothing in the human body is more delicate than the heart (al-fu'ad), and none is more pained by the slightest harm touching it. How much more so when the fire of Hell rises over it and overpowers it. Yet the heart, despite the Fire's domination over it, does not burn, for if it burned it would die. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Neither dying therein nor living﴾ [al-A'la 87:13]. The meaning of ittilaʿ (rising over) is that the Fire descends from the flesh to the heart.

The second: the reason the hearts are singled out for this is that they are the seats of disbelief, of corrupt beliefs, and of corrupt intentions. Know also that it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "The Fire consumes its people until, when it rises over their hearts, it stops. Then Allah, exalted is He, restores their flesh and bones a second time."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾, al-Hasan said: "Mu'sadah" means "closed," from aṣadtu al-bāba and awṣadtuhu, which are two dialects. He did not say "muṭbaqah" (sealed/covered), because al-mu'sadah refers to closed doors, and sealing (al-ițbāq) does not convey the meaning of a door.

Know that the verse conveys intensification of punishment in several respects:

The first: His saying "ليُنْبَذَنَّ" (they will surely be thrown, [al-Humazah 104:4]) implies that it is a place with a very deep bottom, like a well.

The second: had He willed, He could have made that place without any door. But by having a door, it reminds them of the possibility of exit, which increases their grief.

The third: He said ﴿upon them, closed﴾ and did not say "closed upon them." Because His saying ﴿ʿalayhim muʾṣadah﴾ indicates that the primary intent is their being in this state, whereas "muʾṣadah ʿalayhim" does not convey this meaning as the primary intent.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿in pillars stretched out﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: it has been recited as ﴿fi ʿumudin﴾ with two dammas, as ﴿ʿumdin﴾ with the mim sukun, and as ﴿ʿamadin﴾ with two fathas. Al-Farra' said: ʿumud, ʿumd and ʿamad are like adim, udm and adam (hide), ihab, uhb and ahab (skin), and ʿaqim, uqm and aqam (barren). Al-Mubarrad and Abu ʿAli said: ʿumd is the plural of ʿamud (pillar) used for a non-singular form. As for the plural of the singular form, it is ʿumud, like zabur, zubur (psalm, psalms), and rasul, rusul (messenger, messengers).

The second issue: the ʿamud (pillar) is any elongated piece of wood or iron, and it is the foundation of a building. It is said: ʿamud al-bayt (the pillar of the house) for that which the house stands upon.

The third issue: there are two interpretations of the verse.

The first: they are pillars with which those doors are locked, in the manner that alleys are locked. The "fi" (in) here means "bi" (with), meaning: it is closed over them with pillars stretched across it. It did not say "bi-ʿamad" (with pillars) because, due to their number, it became as though the door were within them.

The second view: the meaning is ﴿Indeed it is closed over them﴾ while they are ﴿in pillars﴾ bound, like the stocks in which thieves are confined. O Allah, protect us from them, O Most Generous of the generous.
